sourceInformation.genre: Stealth investigation / crime drama, with a corner-management sim (playing the crew) and an asymmetric hidden-identity versus mode
sourceInformation.perspective: Isometric 2.5D over a 72x56-cell West Baltimore neighborhood (camera turns in 90-degree steps); brawler-view interiors; HTML case-file screens for the Board, notebook, wire room, box and affidavit
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.1 full engine (canvas 2D lighting, E.Shell HTML HUD, E.Dialog, E.Suspicion, FlowField, shapes as data); AI Hub session client 1.4.0; vanilla JavaScript in one IIFE; Web Audio; bundled by a Node script into one HTML file
sourceInformation.artDirection: Engine-native retro-modern pixel art (PS1-era 2D) pushed toward grit: sodium streetlights, rain, Formstone and brick rowhouses, boarded vacants, phone wires with sneakers over the corner, neon store signs; case-file manila, corkboard and phosphor-green wire-room UI
sourceInformation.animation: Engine-native procedural Humanoid rigs (walk/run/crouch, engine poses for sitting, phoning, camera-raise, hands up, cuffed), live portraits in dialogue and polaroids, tweens and timers; no frame lists
sourceInformation.audio: Code-written chip music in the engine's song format with layered tension (8 songs), synthesized effects (shutter, pager, DTMF tones, sirens, cuffs, fence rattles), filtered-noise ambience beds, and Animalese-style gibberish voices from formant grains synced to typed text, with a telephone filter on the wire
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, shared-world versus for 1-4 players (host-authoritative sim, 10 Hz snapshots under 1,100 bytes, client-reported movement with host speed checks, validated actions, leave-to-bot, server host, finish with standings/scores/stats/awards); local split-screen versus for 2; no other network use
sourceInformation.testing: Lightweight, token-efficient: headless Node vm tests (boot, every story beat, attract reel loops, a bots-only versus round, corner ledger, cipher, photo scoring, perception targets, box thresholds, affidavit scoring, montage on every branch, flow tests); Playwright Chromium runs driven only by real key presses and mouse events, steered by the on-screen objective: Episode 1 in one continuous run from the title; Episodes 2, 3 and 4 each in one continuous run from Episode select; Episode 5 in one continuous run down each ending (the raid, and follow the money with the long lens), each to the montage; a simulated DualSense (glyphs, Xbox setting, stick inversion); WebKit iPhone touch-only notice and attract; AI Hub harness all four runs passed; viewport-matrix (2 phones, 5 desktops). No physical controller, no real iOS Safari.
sourceInformation.research: my-3D2dge handoff docs (API.md, parts of AI_GUIDE.md, ASSETS.md, the stealth kit and template) and the AI Hub protocol README; the provided PLAN.md; knowledge of the series from memory; no other web research
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown

testingFeedback: About 33. Real-input play found most of the late ones: Szabo out of talk range; the crew never looking at the street (no face photo possible); Dana pushed out of her car and unable to shoot from cover; the car's view blocked by a building; the mouse unable to pan to Corey; no more film; no marker on the role-read objective; Esc on a screen also pausing the game; the cipher station counting as done without a decode, softlocking the affidavit; Episode select's Episode 2 state missing Pockets' statement; tackles only counting while moving; Tee's payphone stop inside the bus shelter (the tail could never finish); the raid's search spots invisible; the tail retry dropping the player inside a payphone; and dialogue started over an open screen (the call to Dana's mother from the wire room) never advancing.
Twenty would block a player, including every one of the real-input finds except the missing marker and the tackle rule.
Driving the real game in Chromium with only key presses and mouse events, steered by the on-screen objective, with a stall watchdog that dumped state and a screenshot.
Headless flow tests that teleport the player and set facts directly: they proved no code path deadlocks but missed every reachability, sightline and collision problem a real player hits.
engineFeedback: How much comes for free and works the same headless: the standard pause/settings/controls/saves, E.Shell's HUD, E.Suspicion, sight cones, flow fields and a fixed-step clock that made deterministic Node tests easy.

Yes: I assumed shape materials accepted names like 'rusted' and 'linen' as patterns (they are materials, not patterns), and I first missed that pointer events don't report a second mouse button, so left-click while holding right never reached the input.

The wire room (call scheduler, minimization windows, spot-checks, logging key lines in time, voice ID) and the DOM UI kit with spatial focus navigation, hover focus and device-following glyph legends.
Knowing what exists in a very large API: the index is huge, so finding the right call (toCell's return shape, mouseGround, input.held) took grepping and small experiments.
The error reporting that dedupes repeated errors: it hides how often something fails, which misled my first tests; I would overhaul it to keep a count per message.
Built-in chorded mouse button support (and a documented way to read raw gamepad axes for a second stick), so watch-and-shoot schemes work with a mouse out of the box.
promptFeedback: It asks for a complete vertical slice with real infrastructure (attract mode, AI Hub, controller-first UX, an About screen) rather than a toy, and the plan it came with was specific enough to build from.
The plan targeted a 60-75 minute five-episode game with a different file name and model; at medium effort scoping that down while keeping every system was a judgment call the prompt leaves open.

Fitting every system (field surveillance, chase, tail, box, cipher, affidavit and judge, wire room, the corner as Tee, versus with networking, attract) into one coherent, working build in a single session.
A real human playthrough of the full story on a TV with a DualSense, start to credits, to judge pacing and readability at 10 feet.

aiHub.name: WIRETAP
aiHub.description: Work both sides of a West Baltimore corner in 2004: build a wiretap case one photo, page and phone call at a time, then run the corner the case is built on. Includes a 1-4 player cops-vs-corner versus mode.
aiHub.controls: Stick/WASD move · L2/right mouse watch · R2/left click photo · Cross/E interact · Triangle/Q partner, orders, call out · Create/Tab notebook
